title: Keeping Your Eye on the Job
hook: Chidi's contract pays more. His regulars hired the truck for Tuesday, not lunch.
counterintuition: A change that passes every internal review can still abandon the buyer's job. Even though it looks locally harmless, the job-first test is not applied automatically; it has to be a required step before approval.
tryThisNow: Name a change approved last month without asking the job question. Write what it improved internally. Then write whether it made the buyer's progress more or less protected. If both answers are positive, check your work.
keyTakeaway: Apply the job-first test to every proposed change before approving: ask not whether it improves internally, but whether it makes the buyer's progress clearer, safer, faster, or more complete.

breakdown.fastRead:
Chidi has a corporate catering contract that would take his food truck off his regular corner three days a week. The revenue model says yes. His regular customers are not hiring lunch. They are hiring the steady midweek punctuation, the truck being there on Tuesday when the week gets hard. The contract is not a growth win. It is a job-abandonment decision wearing the disguise of a revenue gain.

This is what drift looks like from the inside: a change that improves something real, passes every obvious review, and still abandons the job buyers hired. Keeping focus on the job means applying the job-first test before approving the change, not after.
breakdown.deepRead:
The job-first test asks one question about any proposed change: does this make the buyer's desired progress more or less protected? It is not the same as asking whether the change is good for the business. Internal improvements, cost reductions, and revenue expansions can all pass internal review while failing the job-first test.

Olivier faces this in a bootcamp curriculum review. An alumni advisory board member is direct: "The ML module takes six weeks from fundamentals. That's six weeks of job-ready time spent on terminology that impresses hiring managers who don't actually hire bootcamp grads for ML." The job buyers hired is ready to contribute to a working codebase in week one. The drift is optimizing for what sounds impressive instead of testing every module against the employment job. Nobody made a bad decision in isolation. Each module addition was defensible. The job-first test was never required as a gate.

Drift is hardest to see when the change is genuinely positive in one dimension. A biweekly ordering cycle that cuts logistics costs by 14 percent is a real improvement. A weekly rhythm that lets members know what will be on the shelf Sunday is also real. When those two conflict, the job-first test asks which one the buyer hired. If 38 percent of survey comments reference shelf predictability, the buyer may have hired the weekly rhythm, not the biweekly savings. The test has to be applied before the decision is framed as purely operational.

The job-first test requires someone to ask the question, have authority to require a job-framed answer, and be willing to block approvals when the answer is absent or evasive. That is organizational discipline, not individual insight.

The test has to happen before approval, not in the postmortem.
breakdown.fullRead:
Most organizations apply tests at the end of a decision process. Did we hit budget? Did the feature ship on time? Did client satisfaction hold? These are reasonable measures, but they are all internal. The job-first test is different because it is applied before the decision is finalized, and it measures the change against the buyer's progress rather than the company's operations. The job-first test is not applied automatically; it has to be a required step before approval, especially when the change looks locally harmless.

Laura's architecture firm has a new virtual walkthrough tool. Feedback cycles shortened. The visualization improved. The hospital facilities director said in a side conversation: "The walkthroughs are beautiful. But I don't know what I'm approving anymore." The tool improved a real thing. It also blurred the approval-readiness job. The client's job is not to see a beautiful building. The client's job is to reach a point where they know what they are signing off on. Laura is weighing whether to deploy before applying the job-first test, and the side conversation is the only signal that something may be off.

Here is a useful provocation: think about the last change your own team made that was internally celebrated. Did anyone ask whether it made the buyer's job easier to complete, or just whether it improved a metric you were already measuring? In most teams, the internal metric review happened and the job question was not required. That asymmetry is how drift accumulates.

Tomas's non-emergency routing change passed every available internal test. Response times stayed within acceptable range. Overtime costs dropped. The protocol looked like a straightforward operational improvement. Three months later, a kitchen fire escalated because a non-duty responder hit a roster gap the protocol created. The job-first test was not applied before approval: does this make reliable emergency response more or less protected? The answer might have been visible in scenario modeling if the question had been required. It was not required, so it was not asked.

Nina is holding the recommendation for the cooperative grocery store. Biweekly ordering cuts logistics costs by 14 percent. Thirty-eight percent of member survey comments reference knowing what will be on the shelf Sunday. The weekly rhythm creates a predictability contract. Biweekly breaks that job even as it improves the operational one. The job-first test is available before the recommendation goes forward. Whether it gets applied is a question of organizational discipline, not data availability.

The discipline is a simple requirement: before any proposed change is approved, someone must state the buyer's job in one sentence and answer whether the change makes that job more or less protected. If the answer is uncertain, the approval is deferred until the uncertainty is resolved. This is not a guarantee of perfect decisions. It is a guarantee that the buyer's job is a required input to every decision, not an afterthought when the damage is already done.

examples.title: Laura hears the facilities director doesn't know what he's approving

planSpec.stakes: visualization improvement blurred the approval-readiness job
planSpec.requiredBeat: beautiful walkthroughs improve visualization while blurring the approval-readiness job; Laura faces whether to deploy before applying the job-first test

examples.scenario: Laura sits with the walkthrough demo open on the conference room screen, the hospital facilities director scrolling backward through the rendered corridor. "The walkthroughs are beautiful," he says. "But I don't know what I'm approving anymore." Feedback cycles shortened. The visualization improved. The comment arrives in a side conversation, not a formal complaint. Laura must decide whether to deploy the enhanced walkthrough before applying the job-first test to a change that already has positive internal signals.
examples.whatToDo: State the approval-readiness job before deploying the tool. Ask whether the walkthrough makes the signing-off moment clearer or less clear before it becomes the standard for this account.
examples.whyItMatters: A tool can improve a real thing, like visualization or feedback speed, and still weaken the job the client hired for. The job-first test must be applied before deployment, not after the client signals confusion.

examples.title: Olivier hears six weeks of fundamentals that impress the wrong people

planSpec.stakes: impressive content optimizes against the employment job
planSpec.requiredBeat: ML module takes six weeks from job-ready time to serve impressiveness, not the employment job

examples.scenario: "The ML module takes six weeks from fundamentals," the alumni advisory board member says. "That's six weeks of job-ready time spent on terminology that impresses hiring managers who don't actually hire bootcamp grads for ML." Olivier leans forward with the curriculum map. The module scores well on student surveys. Employers in the advisory group rated the graduates as technically current. The job buyers hired: ready to contribute to a working codebase in week one. Olivier is about to respond to the feedback.
examples.whatToDo: Apply the job-first test to every module in the curriculum: does this content make graduates more or less ready to contribute to a working codebase in week one? Modules that serve impressiveness over readiness are drift candidates.
examples.whyItMatters: Curriculum additions that impress the wrong audience are a form of job drift. The test is not whether the content is valuable in the abstract but whether it serves the job the buyer hired.

examples.title: Tomas implements the routing change and finds the roster gap three months later

planSpec.stakes: overtime optimization was approved without applying the job-first test to emergency reliability
planSpec.requiredBeat: non-emergency routing reduces overtime; three months later a fire escalates through a roster gap the protocol created

examples.scenario: At 11:55 p.m., Tomas signs off on the non-emergency routing change. Response times stay within acceptable range. Overtime costs drop 11 percent. He predicts a clean operational win. Three months later, a kitchen fire escalates. A non-duty responder hit a roster gap the routing protocol created. The postmortem is not about the fire. It is about the question that was not required before approval: does this change make reliable emergency response more or less protected? Tomas must decide whether to require the job-first question in all future routing approvals.
examples.whatToDo: Before approving any protocol change, apply the job-first test: state the job (reliable emergency response) and require an answer about whether the change protects that job across the range of scenarios the department faces.
examples.whyItMatters: A change can pass every available operational test and still fail the job-first test if the test was never required. In emergency services, the postmortem arrives at a cost that cannot be recovered.

examples.title: Andrew finds the case library serving presentations, not client advice

planSpec.stakes: case library serves the consultant's presentation job, not the advisory judgment job
planSpec.requiredBeat: library scores positively internally; consultants use it for presentations; advisory judgment job went underserved

examples.scenario: At 2:00 p.m., Andrew reviews the case library metrics a year after deployment. Internal scores are positive. Consultants rate it useful. Client satisfaction held flat. He pulls the usage logs: the library is used most heavily in the 48 hours before client presentations. It is not showing up in the project work phases where recommendations are formed. The firm is hired to give clients advice they cannot generate internally. The library is being used to prepare how advice looks, not to improve what the advice is.
examples.whatToDo: Restate the firm's job before reviewing the library's design. For each feature, ask: does this help consultants form better recommendations or just present them more confidently? Redirect toward the former.
examples.whyItMatters: A tool that earns high internal scores while serving a secondary job is a drift signal, not a success signal. The job-first test applied after deployment is better than never, but it is costlier than applying it before launch.

examples.title: Nina faces the shelf-predictability contract before the recommendation goes forward

planSpec.stakes: 14 percent logistics savings conflicts with the member's predictability job
planSpec.requiredBeat: biweekly ordering improves logistics cost; 38 percent of member comments reference shelf predictability; Nina faces the recommendation decision

examples.scenario: You are Nina, preparing the recommendation for the cooperative's ordering cycle review. The biweekly shift cuts logistics costs by 14 percent. The member survey is open on your screen: 38 percent of comments reference knowing what will be on the shelf this Sunday. The weekly rhythm is not just a preference; it is the predictability contract members hired the cooperative for. Biweekly breaks that job even as it improves the operational one. Your recommendation is due before the board meeting closes. You must choose whether to recommend the biweekly shift or hold the weekly rhythm.
examples.whatToDo: Apply the job-first test before the recommendation: state the member's job (predictable shelf access), then evaluate whether the logistics saving is worth disrupting the contract members hired the cooperative for.
examples.whyItMatters: A logistics improvement that disrupts a job members hired for is not a straightforward operational win. The job-first test makes the tradeoff visible before it is approved, not after members start shopping elsewhere.

examples.title: Chidi frames the catering contract as a job-abandonment question

planSpec.stakes: catering revenue growth is actually a job-abandonment decision
planSpec.requiredBeat: regular customers hired predictable midweek presence, not lunch; the contract is a job-abandonment decision

examples.scenario: When did you last ask what your regulars actually hired you for? Chidi is holding a corporate catering contract that would take the truck off his regular corner three days a week. The revenue model says yes without hesitation. The regulars who appear at noon on Tuesday are not hiring lunch. They are hiring the predictable midweek punctuation, the truck being there when the week gets hard. The catering contract is a job-abandonment decision wearing the disguise of a revenue gain. Chidi must decide whether to take the contract or hold his corner.
examples.whatToDo: Apply the job-first test before signing: state the job regulars hired the truck for. If three days away per week makes that job less reliably delivered, name the contract as a tradeoff and decide it deliberately.
examples.whyItMatters: Revenue growth that abandons the job buyers hired for is not growth of the business they hired. The job-first test makes the abandonment decision visible so it can be made intentionally.

questions.prompt: A software tool improves feedback cycle speed for an architecture client. A facilities director says in a side conversation that he no longer knows what he is approving. What does this reveal about the proposed change?
choices: The feedback cycle improvement was not large enough to matter to the client.
The client's preference for slower tools should be accommodated as a service exception.
The change improved one internal metric while weakening the buyer's approval-readiness job.
questions.explanation: Faster feedback cycles and clearer approval readiness can point in different directions. The side conversation is the signal that the job-first test was not applied before the tool was deployed.

questions.prompt: A coding bootcamp's ML module earns strong student survey scores but uses six weeks of time that advisors say should be spent on job-ready fundamentals. What should the program director do before the next curriculum cycle?
choices: Apply the job-first test to every module: ask whether each one makes graduates more or less ready to contribute to a working codebase in week one.

Strong student survey scores are the most reliable signal of curriculum quality and should be weighted heavily: satisfaction predicts completion rates and referral behavior, both of which drive program revenue, and a curriculum change that produces lower satisfaction scores would impose financial costs that outweigh any week-one readiness improvement, making survey performance the right gate for module retention decisions.

Survey the companies that hire graduates and produce a ranked list of technical topics they consider most important in the first sixty days, then compare that list to the current curriculum to identify gaps, treating the labor market's stated preferences as the external standard that defines job readiness rather than relying on an internal test applied by the program director.
questions.explanation: Strong internal survey scores do not confirm the module serves the employment job. The job-first test requires asking whether the content serves the buyer's progress, not whether students find it interesting.

questions.prompt: A volunteer fire department changes non-emergency routing to reduce overtime. Response times stay within range. Three months later, a fire escalates because of a roster gap the protocol created. What was missing from the approval process?
choices: A financial review of the overtime savings against the long-term cost of emergency escalation.
A required job-first test asking whether the protocol change made reliable emergency response more or less protected.
A committee vote on whether the overtime savings were worth the operational risk.
questions.explanation: The approval process had operational and financial tests but not the job-first test. Requiring that test before approval would have forced the question of emergency reliability into the decision.

questions.prompt: A consulting firm's case library earns high internal scores. Usage logs show it is used primarily before presentations, not during recommendation development. Client satisfaction is flat. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
choices: Client satisfaction is a lagging indicator and will improve as consultants use the library more.
The library was built for the consultant's presentation job instead of the advisory judgment job the firm is hired to deliver.
The library needs more content before it can affect recommendation quality.
questions.explanation: High internal scores and frequent use do not confirm the tool serves the buyer's job. The usage pattern reveals which job the tool actually serves, and it is not the one that produces client satisfaction.

questions.prompt: A cooperative grocery store can shift to biweekly ordering and cut logistics costs by 14 percent. Thirty-eight percent of member comments reference knowing what will be on the shelf each Sunday. Before approving the change, what does the job-first test require?
choices: Calculate whether the 14 percent saving is large enough to compensate dissatisfied members.
Survey members on whether they prefer cost savings or shelf predictability.
State the member's job explicitly and answer whether biweekly ordering makes that job more or less protected.
questions.explanation: The job-first test requires naming the job before evaluating the change. A savings calculation and a preference survey both skip the step of defining what buyers hired the cooperative to deliver.

questions.prompt: A food truck operator is offered a corporate catering contract that would take the truck off its regular corner three days a week. The revenue is meaningful. What does the job-first test ask before the contract is signed?
choices: Whether the catering revenue can be reinvested in marketing to attract new regular customers.
Whether the contract requires the truck to leave the corner on the days regulars show up most.
Whether three days away per week makes the predictable midweek presence job more or less reliably delivered for regular customers.
questions.explanation: The job regulars hired for is not lunch; it is a predictable presence at a specific time. The job-first test asks whether the contract change protects or abandons that job, not whether the revenue is attractive.

questions.prompt: A team says its job is still the priority and that the new process change aligns with it. A manager wants to test whether this is true. What distinguishes a tested claim from a stated one?
choices: The team can show that the change, when traced through the buyer's path, makes their desired progress clearer or more complete.

The test is stakeholder alignment: if other functions and senior leadership independently assess the change as consistent with the job, the claim is validated because systematic misalignment across multiple perspectives would surface as explicit disagreement, and when no one in the review chain objects on job-protection grounds, the claim should be treated as confirmed without requiring a formal buyer-path trace.

The test is post-deployment outcome metrics: the relevant performance indicators should be measured before and after the change is deployed, and if they improve, the claim that the job was protected is confirmed, because pre-deployment tracing is ultimately speculative without real user behavior to validate it and outcome measurement produces cleaner evidence.
questions.explanation: Stating that the job is a priority is not the same as testing whether a specific change serves it. The test requires tracing the change through the buyer's progress, not through the internal strategy document.

questions.prompt: A team discovers in a postmortem that a change approved six months ago was actually a job-abandonment decision. They want to prevent this in the future. Which process change is most likely to help?
choices: Require that every proposed change include a statement of the buyer's job and an answer to whether the change makes that job more or less protected, before approval.

Require a structured postmortem within 60 days of each major launch: teams run a standard debrief that includes a standing question about whether the buyer's job was protected, creating a feedback loop that identifies job-abandonment decisions after the fact and builds institutional memory without adding a pre-approval gate that slows development velocity.

Add a jobs-focused advisory role in the approval chain: a designated reviewer whose specific accountability is flagging job-abandonment risk before any proposal is approved, so that line teams submit proposals normally and the specialist provides the jobs lens, rather than requiring every team to write a jobs statement they may compose poorly due to limited familiarity with the framework.
questions.explanation: A postmortem finds the problem after the damage is done. Requiring the job-first test before approval prevents the decision from being made without the buyer's job as a required input.

questions.prompt: An operations director argues that a new efficiency initiative is not a job question because it only affects internal processes. What is the strongest counterargument?
choices: Internal processes always affect buyers directly, so no process change is purely internal.
The efficiency initiative may pass every internal test while changing how buyers experience the path to their desired progress.
Internal process changes are exempt from the job-first test if they do not touch customer-facing features.
questions.explanation: The job-first test applies to any change that affects the buyer's path, including internal processes that alter handoffs, timing, or quality. Whether a change is internal does not determine whether it affects the buyer's job.

reviewCards.front: A change passed every internal review. How do you apply the job-first test?
reviewCards.back: State the buyer's job in one sentence and ask whether the change makes that job clearer, safer, faster, or more complete. Internal approval does not answer this question.

reviewCards.front: A tool improves something real and earns positive internal scores. What signal suggests drift?
reviewCards.back: Check how buyers are using it and whether client outcomes improved. High internal scores combined with flat or declining buyer outcomes indicate the tool serves an internal job, not the buyer's job.

reviewCards.front: What distinguishes stating that the job is a priority from testing it?
reviewCards.back: A stated priority appears in documents and presentations. A tested priority requires tracing each proposed change through the buyer's path and showing that the change makes their desired progress more protected, not just that it aligns with stated strategy.

reviewCards.front: A revenue opportunity conflicts with the buyer's job. What does the job-first test require?
reviewCards.back: Name the conflict explicitly before approving. The test does not prohibit taking the opportunity, but it requires the abandonment decision to be made intentionally, not by default, with the job clearly named as the cost.

reviewCards.front: Where in the decision process should the job-first test be applied?
reviewCards.back: Before approval, not in a postmortem. The test is most valuable when it is a required input to the decision, not a retrospective explanation of why something did not work after the change was already made.

implementationPlan.title: Applying the Job-First Test to Changes
implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is applying the job-first test as a required gate before approving any change, not as an optional reflection afterward. This requires naming the buyer's job in one sentence and testing the proposed change against it.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a proposed change is presented without a statement of the buyer's job, then require the proposer to add that statement and answer whether the change makes that job more or less protected before the review continues.
If a new health routine improvement looks appealing, then write the job the routine is hired for and ask whether the improvement makes that job easier to complete or just easier to report.
If a new opportunity would require dropping something regular customers or users rely on, then name the job they hired you for before calculating the revenue or efficiency gain.
If a change to a regular commitment seems harmless on paper, then ask the other person what they hired that commitment for before deciding the change is safe.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, take one change currently under consideration and apply the job-first test in writing: state the buyer's job in one sentence, describe what the change improves internally, and write a clear answer to whether the change makes the buyer's job more or less protected.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, review one approved change from the past month and ask whether the job-first test was applied before approval. If it was not, write what the test would have asked and whether the answer would have changed the decision.

memorableLines.text: The contract is not a growth win. It is a job-abandonment decision wearing the disguise of a revenue gain.
memorableLines.why: It names the disguise that makes drift hard to see and gives it a precise label.

memorableLines.text: The job-first test is not applied automatically; it has to be a required step before approval, especially when the change looks locally harmless.
memorableLines.why: It explains why good intentions are not sufficient and why the test must be structural.

memorableLines.text: The test has to be applied before the decision is framed as purely operational.
memorableLines.why: It identifies the precise moment when the test can still change the outcome.
